newsitem.title: BERMUDA: After handover, Bermuda is jewel in a small crown.
newsitem.headline: After handover, Bermuda is jewel in a small crown.

text.p: As the Union Jack was lowered on Hong Kong for the last time, Bermuda on Monday assumed the status of Britain's most populous and prosperous remaining overseas possession.

Bermudans gathered around television sets to watch live pictures of the pageantry of the handover ceremonies several oceans away. The event was front-page news in the leading newsaper, The Royal Gazette.
"What a great ceremony. Only the British could put on a display like that," one resident said.
"It's the lead story on the island. There's special interest here," he added. "There's a serious awareness that Bermuda is now the biggest and most prosperous part of what's left of the empire."

Bermuda, population 61,000, is also Britain's oldest colony. Lying in the Atlantic 580 miles (930 km) east of North Carolina, it was settled after a ship of settlers headed for Virginia foundered on its reefs in 1609.
It is governed by a royal governor and has the oldest legislative body among British dependencies, Hong Kong's now-defunct elected assembly included.

The other remnants of Britain's once-great empire are Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, Montserrat, and the Turks and Caicos Islands in the Caribbean; Gibralta in the Mediterrean; the British Indian Ocean Territory; the Pitcairn Islands in the South Pacific; St. Helena, the Falkland Islands, and South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands in the South Atlantic; and the British Antarctic Territory.
While the eyes of the world focused on Hong Kong, a senior member of the ruling United Bermuda Party made a strong plea for Bermuda's independence on Monday.

"Independence is an issue that will not go away," Sen. Larry Scott told Reuters. "I would hope to see an independent Bermuda as soon as possible. We need something other than the colonial context to govern us as we move into the new millennium."

But the issue is not a burning one. Unlike the people of Hong Kong, who had no say in their fate during negotiations between Beijing and London, Bermudans had a referendum on independence in August 1995, and voters rejected the notion. Premier Pamela Gordon says the matter is not on the agenda.
A number of British expatriates in Bermuda are old Hong Kong hands who indulged in a bout of nostalgia on Monday as the Asian outpost became part of China after 156 years of British rule.

Like Hong Kong, Bermuda has prospered as a financial centre. Nearly 10,000 foreign companies are based here. One of them is Jardine Matheson, "the princely hong" founded by Scottish traders whose story is intertwined with Hong Kong's since the Opium Wars with China in the last century.

In 1984 Jardines, by then Hong Kong's largest private-sector employee, infuriated Beijing when it shifted its base to Bermuda almost before the ink was dry on the Sino-British agreement that handed the colony back.
Bermuda is thriving, one resident said, but he added, "We are more discreet than Hong Kong."
